options: Avocado rancher with a hobby shop
fact: Self-taught woodworker Sam Maloof, the first craftsman to win a MacArthur 'genius' grant, kept adding rooms, shops and studio included, until his 6-room house had 16 more. Then a new freeway was routed right through it, so in 2000 the whole house was moved about 3 miles.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Shopkeepers who also run the hotel
fact: As St. Elmo's mines died, the Stark family bought up the empty buildings to save them, a big reason this ghost town still stands. Annabelle, the last Stark, kept this place going as a 16-room boarding house, store, post office and telegraph desk into the 1950s.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Artist J. André Smith founded this experimental art colony in 1937 with money from philanthropist Mary Curtis Bok, and painters like Milton Avery came to work here. He wrapped it in Maya-inspired ornament, and it's now a National Historic Landmark and one of the Southeast's rare 'Mayan Revival' buildings.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: One of the earliest prefab houses in the U.S., it arrived by steamship and mule cart in 1873, with its frame on the outside and the finish inside, hence the nickname 'Inside-Outside House'. Retired sea captain Pierce ran a cabinet shop downstairs, lived upstairs, and later became a bank president.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Banker Samuel Nickerson spent four years and $450,000 on this 'Marble Palace', reportedly Chicago's most expensive home when it was finished in 1883. Note the vault; the American College of Surgeons later took it over, and today it's the Driehaus Museum.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Killer family with a guest room
fact: Charles Reynolds bought this plaza store-and-home in 1903 and remodeled it on borrowed money, including a mortgage from the parish priest. In 1913 the priest foreclosed, moved in, taught catechism in the store, and later left the whole place to his housekeeper.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Railroad lawyer with a big library
fact: Jasper Cropsey trained as an architect before going all-in on blazing autumn landscapes, and he even designed stations for New York's elevated railways. This was the Hudson River School painter's last home and studio.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: John Carter learned printing as an apprentice to Benjamin Franklin, then ran the Providence Gazette 'at the sign of Shakespeare's Head' and the post office from this house. His reporting on the Gaspee Affair got him arrested for libel.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

labels.t: ROOMS ON FIRST FLOOR PROBABLY USED AS PRINTING OFFICE AND POST OFFICE

fact: Painter Sydney Burleigh built this studio building in 1885, and artists still work in it. H. P. Lovecraft made it the home of the young sculptor in 'The Call of Cthulhu'; when an editor who'd once lived there jokingly vowed to send a ghost at 3 a.m., Lovecraft wrote a poem at 3 a.m. that night.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: In 1882 investors from Dundee, Scotland bought this Texas ranch for $1.25 million and ran it for seven decades. Their guest house was nicknamed the 'Scotsman's Dive', and by about 1925 it held the offices of the ranch manager and bookkeeper.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Society couple with a music room
fact: Cattle-ranch heiress Electra Waggoner met her husband while traveling in the Himalayas, and this mansion was built for the couple in 1903-04. A Texas town was named after her; the Whartons sold the house in 1911 to another cattle baron.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Henry Field owned a brickyard, and his maker's mark, cut into the brick molds, still shows up reversed on the paving bricks out front. In 1919 his company's president, Andrés Pacheco, took over the property, and Pacheco daughters still lived upstairs when HABS came.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Botanist printing the paper at home
fact: Ferdinand Lindheimer fled Germany after a failed 1833 uprising, was shipwrecked, and reached Texas the day after the battle of San Jacinto. The 'Father of Texas Botany' also edited the town's German-language newspaper, printed right here in his house.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Mogul with big brood and butler
Bachelor mine owner with a library
fact: Alfred McCune built railroads, went into Peruvian mines with J.P. Morgan and Hearst, and in 1900 built this 21-room mansion with servants' stair and butler's pantry. His 1899 Senate run deadlocked the legislature so badly that Utah sent no senator to Washington at all.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Painter who ended up a grocer
Dude-ranch cook with a food stand
fact: Harrison Crandall served as Grand Teton's official park photographer, selling prints and postcards of the peaks to visitors. He built this studio cabin in 1925-26, then tacked on a bedroom and a grocery store.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Chicago's park bosses ousted Jens Jensen in 1900 for refusing to go along with graft, and he came back to run the whole West Park system. The 'dean of the Prairie style' of landscape design used this kitchen as his drafting studio.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Modernist Paul Schweikher built this as his own home and studio from 1938, complete with a Zen garden and a solar dressing room. He went on to chair the Yale School of Architecture.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: A radical free-thinker, anti-slavery journal was printed here, and its voice helped keep Missouri's Germans with the Union. Then Carl Strehly went into wine: cellar, tavern, and an upstairs dance hall.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

options: Tobacco farmer with a tool shed
fact: Fancy Victorian brackets outside, but inside it's the old three-room Pennsylvania German plan with separate doors for parlor and kitchen; a rear addition held a luncheonette and grocery until about 1950. In 1977 the Army Corps of Engineers demolished it for a reservoir project.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Swiss merchant Conrad Meuly hauled $1,600 of goods on the Texan Santa Fe Expedition, was taken prisoner, and lost it all. He started over as a Corpus Christi baker and grocer and built this house and store with concrete-brick walls.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Joseph Barton bet a railroad was coming, founded a town named after himself, and bought this house's plans for $45 from a magazine. The railroad never came through, and his showpiece, meat-and-milk cooler and all, ended up anchoring a town that faded away.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Artist Frederic Bartlett got this beachfront land as a wedding gift from his father-in-law and designed the whole estate himself with no architecture training. His widow Evelyn, ex-wife of Eli Lilly, kept wintering here until 1997; giving it away was the largest single private donation in Florida history.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Peter Britt hauled 300 pounds of camera gear down the Oregon Trail, until his own wagon train split over it, and reached the gold camp with five dollars. Note the skylit studio: his Crater Lake photos helped get it made a national park.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: William Jackson became the first keeper in 1869, with his wife Caroline as official assistant keeper: $1,000 a year between them. The lamp first burned lard, and every night someone had to haul the fuel up the tower.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Keeper Emmanuel Luick's wife Ella turned the official logbook into her personal diary. When he fell ill for three weeks in 1901, she nursed him by day and kept the light burning by night.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Jacob Wohlfarth, a former Menger Hotel chef, put up a wood-frame general store with a camp yard here in the 1880s and lived on site. It stood, much modified, until the early 1990s, and archaeologists later dug the lot hunting for a lost irrigation ditch.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Bill Menor homesteaded alone on the Snake River in 1892, ran a ferry, and tacked a store onto the east end of his cabin. When his brother Holiday moved in across the river in 1905, the two didn't speak for two years, yet Bill made his whitewash from Holiday's lime pit.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Conrad Beissel's Ephrata Cloister (1732) ran on extreme self-denial: members slept on 15-inch wooden benches with wooden blocks for pillows and ate one small meal a day. They also rose at midnight for a two-hour watch; this is the Saron, the sisters' house.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: At Watervliet, the first Shaker community, brothers and sisters got their own halves and staircases and sat on opposite sides of the shared meeting room. These celibate believers were also the first to sell seeds in little paper envelopes.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: This stone courthouse, finished in 1815, later served as the county jail. Before the town had a bell, the sheriff climbed the cupola and blew a huge tin horn to call court.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: This gold-camp jail was accepted on April 1, 1870. After the town's first schoolhouse burned in the 1880s, the front room served as the school for a while.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: San Quentin's Dungeon, built 1854, packed 14 tiny cells off one corridor. HABS says it may be the oldest surviving building ever built by the State of California.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Army laundresses were among the few women the Army officially recognized: they got housing and rations, and each soldier paid for his own washing. At Fort Union their 11 rooms sat right next to the guardhouse; in 1883 Congress cut the laundresses altogether.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Family of killers running an inn
fact: The Benders split their tiny Kansas inn and store with a canvas wagon cover, and daughter Kate handed out flyers billing herself as a healer and psychic who held séances. Travelers on that trail kept disappearing; in 1873, as a search closed in, the whole family fled and was never found.
credit: Wichita City Eagle, 1873 · via Wikimedia Commons (newspaper diagram)

options: Con-man killer posing as a hotelier
fact: H. H. Holmes, a Chicago con man and murderer, added a 'hotel' floor for the 1893 World's Fair and refused to pay his architects and suppliers. The papers sold it as a 'Murder Castle' maze, but most of that was invented; its real hidden rooms hid furniture he'd bought on credit and never meant to pay for.
credit: New York World, 1895 · via Wikimedia Commons (newspaper diagram; sensational labels and shading removed)

fact: Built as a rooming house for cigar workers from Spain and Cuba in Tampa's Ybor City. In the 1920s and '30s the café downstairs became a gambling den known for roulette, blackjack and underworld figures, and in the 1920s the upstairs worked as a bordello for the casino's customers. Busy building.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Caffey's Inlet was one of seven U.S. Life-Saving Service stations put on North Carolina's Outer Banks in 1874, off the 'Graveyard of the Atlantic'. The crew of this 1897–98 rebuild kept watch from the tower and hauled rescue boats and carts out to wrecks. It closed in 1964 and is now a beach-resort restaurant.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Milwaukee's Engine House 27 (1903) was designed by Sebastian Brand, a German immigrant who joined the fire department in 1872 and fought more than 5,000 blazes before leaving it in 1903. The crew slept upstairs in the dormitory; the engine waited downstairs for the alarm.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Railroad lawyer with a book habit
fact: Villa Montezuma (San Diego, 1887) was built for Jesse Shepard, a flamboyant, eccentric pianist and singer with worldwide fame. His longest-lasting fame came as an author under the pen name Francis Grierson. The stained glass was just the opening act.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: In 1928 a 'main room' was built onto a 'hod': the mid-ship deckhouse of the barque AMAZON, built in Baltimore in 1853 and set on the shore at Oxford, Maryland. The old deckhouse became the bedroom, one step down from the rest of the house. The house was demolished after 2007.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Edward Elderkin, a young lawyer from the eastern states, arrived in Elkhorn, Wisconsin, in 1839 and built this octagon in 1851. The 1930s HABS write-up calls him 'an eccentric' and says many Wisconsin towns had one of these 'freak houses'. Government paperwork with no chill.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Candy maker with a soda fountain
fact: Charles Lundberg's bakery (1875–76) stood one block from both the Texas Capitol and the Governor's Mansion, and stayed a bakery until 1937. Living quarters upstairs, ovens out back: the shortest commute in Austin.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Saloon keeper living behind the bar
fact: Built in the 1870s at Niobrara's original townsite, it was moved after the 1881 flood. From 1886 it was the drugstore and doctor's office, with living quarters behind the shop; in 1905 it became the office of the Niobrara Tribune.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: The gold prospector it's named after
fact: Everyone calls it Scotty's Castle, and 'Death Valley Scotty' told reporters his secret gold mine paid for it. It was really the vacation home of Chicago insurance magnate Albert Johnson, who had invested in Scotty's mine (it didn't exist) and told the press he was just 'Scotty's banker'.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: The core of this bunkhouse row is two log cabins Johnny Grant built in the early 1860s, joined by an open, roofed dog trot. Conrad Kohrs and John Bielenberg walled in the gap between 1884 and 1890, making a bunk room for about five cowboys. The horses got stalls under the same roof.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: Skykomish, a small mountain town in Washington's Cascades, built this Craftsman house for the teachers of the school next door. It has housed teachers and school staff ever since; today the superintendent and family live here. Homework, delivered next door.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: John Lautner designed this 1957 cabin in the Idyllwild art colony for accomplished amateur musicians who summered there. The heart of it is one round room for music, sitting, cooking and sleeping. Practice, dinner and bedtime: same room.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Around 1860 the Cheshire Mills in Harrisville, New Hampshire, built this boarding house for its single mill workers, closely copying the boarding houses of Lowell, Massachusetts. It kept doing that job until 1965. Room, board and a factory whistle.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

fact: This c.1832 stone house on Washington's National Mall served the lock joining the C&O Canal to the Washington City Canal, which later became an open sewer. Then came a squatters' tenement, a Park Police post with a holding cell, and after WWII a public toilet. Quite a career.
credit: HABS/HAER/HALS, National Park Service · via Wikimedia Commons

options: Texas Ranger captain and his men
Army general before the Civil War
fact: French merchant F. L. des Mazières built this San Antonio store in 1853; upstairs soon became a gaming room. HABS says Gen. David Twiggs used the place as headquarters, the store as his office. In February 1861 Twiggs handed U.S. Army property in Texas to secessionists without a shot fired.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress
q: WHO USED THE STORE AS HIS OFFICE?

fact: In 1908 Charles Spruks bought John Roebling's defunct Delaware Aqueduct, a canal bridge, to reach his timber customers in Pennsylvania, and opened it to the public for a fee. This tollhouse was office and home for the collectors until the 1950s. Tolls ran until 1979.
credit: HAER, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Built in 1854 as two mirror-image units, each with a parlor downstairs and two bedrooms upstairs around one shared chimney. A third keeper came by 1860 and a fourth by 1883. In 1999 the house was moved about half a mile with the lighthouse to escape the eroding shore.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: This 1903 floating summer house in the Thousand Islands was built for George Boldt, manager of New York's Waldorf-Astoria. Too big to pass under the canal bridges, it was built in sections, shipped by rail and assembled at his island estate. Dancing deck upstairs, servants below.
credit: HAER, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: In 1870 the Alaska Commercial Company got an exclusive 20-year U.S. lease to run the seal harvest on the Pribilof Islands. The original Webster House on St. Paul Island housed the overseer at the Northeast Point rookery, and Kipling name-checked it in 'The White Seal' (1894).
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: The basement of the National Zoo's Reptile House in Washington, opened Feb. 27, 1931, under director William Mann; municipal architect Albert Harris gave it a church-like Romanesque look, gargoyles included. 'Brumation' is reptile hibernation. Even the cellar has a dress code.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Built in 1926 of peeled logs, about 20 by 19 feet, this was the first administration building of Mount McKinley (now Denali) National Park. In 1941 staff left the 'dilapidated one room building'; it became a naturalist's museum, was moved twice, and ended up a staff house.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress
q: WHAT WAS THIS CABIN BUILT AS?

fact: Built in 1925 for $35,000 as the home office and studio of H. George Fink, an architect of George Merrick's new Coral Gables, Florida. The roof once carried an Arab riding-camel weathervane. Fink worked here until 1932, sharing it with the Tropical Sales Corporation.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: On Bill Keys' Desert Queen Ranch in today's Joshua Tree National Park, this round tack house began life as a cyanide tank used to process gold ore. Now it holds bridles and harnesses. Desert ranchers waste nothing, not even the poison tank.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress
q: WHAT WAS THIS ROUND SHED FIRST?

fact: Saddleback Ledge Light, Maine, 1839: a granite tower on a bare rock 6 miles by boat from Vinalhaven, cost $15,000. An 1842 report called it the only one in New England by an 'architect and engineer', then noted it had nowhere to collect fresh water or secure the boat.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Office of Dr. John C. Carter in Springdale, Arkansas, built over a spring. Carter went to California in 1854 to seek his fortune, came home and apprenticed as a physician, bought the property in 1871, yet the 1870 census calls him a 'merchant'. His store across the street ran until he died in 1886.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: The Linnaean House at the Missouri Botanical Garden, built 1881-82 as an orangery for a collection of tubbed palm trees. Remodeled in 1919 for camellias and azaleas, it is called probably the oldest greenhouse of its type in continuous use west of the Mississippi.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Financier Paul J. Armour built this octagon in Irvington, NY, in 1859-60. In 1872 Joseph Stiner, a New York City tea importer, bought it for $27,000 and added the dome, the cupola and a veranda that reportedly cost $26,000 by itself. It is one of two domed octagonal houses in the U.S.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress
q: WHO PUT A DOME ON THIS OCTAGON?

fact: J.C. Lore & Sons in Solomons, Maryland, packed oysters from 1888 to 1978, the longest run of any Patuxent River company; this building dates from 1934. Lore was among the first to ship oysters by parcel post. Shuckers' output went up on a tally board.
credit: HAER, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Built in 1847 on Nantucket as a brick oil and candle factory; in 1849 oil merchants William Hadwen and Nathaniel Barney bought it to make sperm candles. Their spermaceti candle press still stands inside: since June 15, 1930 the building has been the island's Whaling Museum.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Hopewell Furnace's office-store, Pennsylvania, believed built around 1784: the center of an iron-making village, the furnace's general office and the shop that supplied everything the workers needed. The drawing notes it was probably meant to be heated by stoves, the furnace's major product.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Built in 1911 on the Arroyo Seco in Los Angeles for USC's College of Fine Arts, after a fire destroyed the school's first building. Its dean was painter William Lees Judson. When USC moved the art school in 1920, it became Judson Studios, a stained-glass firm still run by the family.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: Fuertes Observatory at Cornell, completed 1917 to a design by architecture professor L.P. Burnham, with a 24-foot steel dome over a 12-inch refracting telescope. Generations of students got their first look at the sky here; today light pollution from new dorms nearby dims the view.
credit: HABS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress

fact: In 1985 a couple in Montecito, California, wanted a small building by their pool to entertain friends, change clothes and shower. Landscape architect Isabelle Greene proposed a 'folly' shaped like a Japanese tea house instead of a stucco box; local architect Andy Neumann did the interiors.
credit: HALS, National Park Service · via Library of Congress
q: WHAT IS THIS GARDEN TEA HOUSE REALLY FOR?
